summary.text: At \(n=140\), the floor evaluations \(\lfloor140\sqrt{5/4}\rfloor=156\), \(\lfloor144\sqrt{5/4}\rfloor=160\), \(\lfloor157\sqrt{5/4}\rfloor=175\), and \(\lfloor161\sqrt{5/4}\rfloor=180\) give \(a(140)=471\), \(a(144)=484\), \(a(157)=528\), and \(a(161)=542\). Thus the proposed recurrence would require \(542=528+484-471=541\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\alpha=\sqrt{\frac54}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
a(m)=2m+\lfloor m\alpha\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac m4\right\rfloor
\quad(m\ge 1).
\]
We disprove the proposed recurrence
\[
a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)
\]
by evaluating both sides at \(n=140\).

We first compute the four sequence values that occur in this instance of the recurrence. Since \(\alpha\ge 0\) and
\[
\alpha^2=\frac54,
\]
the floor of each relevant multiple of \(\alpha\) can be determined by comparing squares. For nonnegative real numbers, squaring is strictly increasing, so inequalities between the corresponding squares imply the desired inequalities between the numbers themselves.

For \(m=140\),
\[
(140\alpha)^2=140^2\cdot\frac54=24500.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
156^2=24336<24500<24649=157^2.
\]
All three quantities being compared before squaring are nonnegative, this gives
\[
156<140\alpha<157.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\lfloor140\alpha\rfloor=156.
\]
Also \(140/4=35\), and hence
\[
a(140)=2\cdot140+156+35=280+156+35=471.
\]

For \(m=144\),
\[
(144\alpha)^2=144^2\cdot\frac54=25920.
\]
Moreover,
\[
160^2=25600<25920<25921=161^2.
\]
Thus
\[
160<144\alpha<161,
\]
so
\[
\lfloor144\alpha\rfloor=160.
\]
Since \(144/4=36\), it follows that
\[
a(144)=2\cdot144+160+36=288+160+36=484.
\]

For \(m=157\), it is convenient to keep the square as a fraction:
\[
(157\alpha)^2=157^2\cdot\frac54
=24649\cdot\frac54
=\frac{123245}{4}.
\]
The neighboring integer squares satisfy
\[
175^2=30625=\frac{122500}{4}
<\frac{123245}{4}
<\frac{123904}{4}=30976=176^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
175<157\alpha<176,
\]
and hence
\[
\lfloor157\alpha\rfloor=175.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
39\le \frac{157}{4}<40,
\]
so \(\lfloor157/4\rfloor=39\). We obtain
\[
a(157)=2\cdot157+175+39=314+175+39=528.
\]

Finally, for \(m=161\),
\[
(161\alpha)^2=161^2\cdot\frac54
=25921\cdot\frac54
=\frac{129605}{4}.
\]
Here
\[
180^2=32400=\frac{129600}{4}
<\frac{129605}{4}
<\frac{131044}{4}=32761=181^2.
\]
It follows that
\[
180<161\alpha<181,
\]
so
\[
\lfloor161\alpha\rfloor=180.
\]
Also,
\[
40\le \frac{161}{4}<41,
\]
whence \(\lfloor161/4\rfloor=40\). Thus
\[
a(161)=2\cdot161+180+40=322+180+40=542.
\]

Now specialize the conjectured recurrence to \(n=140\). Since
\[
n+21=161,\qquad n+17=157,\qquad n+4=144,
\]
it would require
\[
a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
But the right-hand side is
\[
528+484-471=541,
\]
whereas the left-hand side is
\[
a(161)=542.
\]
Thus the proposed equality at \(n=140\) would assert \(542=541\), which is false. Since \(140\ge1\), this is an admissible index in the conjecture. Therefore the claimed recurrence does not hold for every \(n\ge1\), and the conjecture is disproved.
